node.label: C. V. Wedgwood
node.description: Combines narrative craft with political, military, biographical and cultural history for broad audiences. She reconstructs participants’ motives and uncertainty, while revising judgments when documents and scholarship change. Her sustained practice gives historical narrative a place during the expansion of social-scientific approaches.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Cicely Veronica Wedgwood; The Thirty Years War (1938); The King’s Peace and The King’s War; biographical work on William the Silent. These are contributions to political, military, and biographical history.
node.scope_note: The King’s Peace (1955) and The King’s War (1958) defend attention to sequence and contemporary experience without answering every causal question. Woolrych documents the 1961 revaluation of Strafford and criticizes occasional eulogy and weak explanation of social/regional allegiance; Parker’s war criticism is mediated through that memoir. Her cultural work includes verse and political imagination. Narrative continuity precedes the 1979 debate; original prefaces and cases are not fully collated here.

incident_edges.relationship: reconstructs seventeenth-century political conflict through narrative histories
incident_edges.evidence_note: Editorial placement based on the cited work or supporting account; not a claim that this historian founded the whole field. Woolrych pp. 529–530 quotes the prefaces on uncertainty, motives and narrative explanation, while noting limits concerning allegiance. Original prefaces remain mediated.

incident_edges.relationship: connects warfare to political and religious conflict in early modern Europe
incident_edges.evidence_note: Editorial placement based on the cited work or supporting account; not a claim that this historian founded the whole field. Woolrych discusses battlefield reconstruction and the relation of campaigns to politics; he also records Parker’s objection to the German-centered framing.

incident_edges.relationship: uses individual political lives alongside wider narratives
incident_edges.evidence_note: Editorial placement based on the cited work or supporting account; not a claim that this historian founded the whole field. Woolrych pp. 523–525 distinguishes early Strafford from the 1961 revaluation prompted by new documents and research.

incident_edges.relationship: provides an earlier example of sustained narrative historical writing
incident_edges.evidence_note: The 1938 work demonstrates narrative continuity, not a narrative practice originating with a 1979 revival. The 1955/1958 prefatory defense, as quoted by Woolrych, supplies a particular methodological comparison. It is not a response to Stone’s later diagnosis.

incident_edges.relationship: Wedgwood participates in Tawney’s economic-history seminar
incident_edges.evidence_note: Woolrych p. 529 documents attendance after graduation. This is a teaching encounter, not proof that her mature narrative adopted Tawney’s causal conclusions.

incident_edges.relationship: Neale advises on structure; Cooper, Kearney and Aylmer contribute to revaluation
incident_edges.evidence_note: Woolrych pp. 523–524 differentiates early advice from later scholarship and newly available documents. Original correspondence and the cited scholars’ cases remain unread.
incident_edges.map_label: Advice and research behind Strafford’s revaluation

incident_edges.relationship: Parker challenges the framing and negative conclusion of The Thirty Years War
incident_edges.evidence_note: Woolrych p. 525 n. 5 attributes criticism to Parker’s 1984 book, pp. xv and 216–217. These original pages are not independently collated; criticism coexists with recognition of the book’s achievement.

incident_edges.relationship: Woolrych questions occasional eulogy and limits of biographical scale
incident_edges.evidence_note: Memoir pp. 523–525 assesses early Strafford and William the Silent while valuing the later revaluation. It is not a claim that all her biographies share one uncorrected flaw.

incident_edges.relationship: Wedgwood connects poetry and visual culture with political imagination
incident_edges.evidence_note: Woolrych p. 532 discusses Poetry and Politics under the Stuarts (1960), including court masques and popular verse. Original cases remain unread; the placement does not imply Burckhardt/Huizinga descent.
